weeks.title: Power BI, your first published dashboard
weeks.context:
Power BI is the tool most BI analyst roles now expect you to know by name. It does three jobs in one: Power Query cleans and reshapes raw data, the data model links tables together with relationships, and DAX measures turn those tables into the numbers a business actually asks for, all feeding a dashboard you can publish to a live URL.

This week you build that whole pipeline end to end on the Sample Superstore dataset: install Power BI Desktop, clean the data in Power Query, build a date dimension and a star schema, write six DAX measures, lay out a one-page dashboard, and publish it to the Power BI Service so it has a real link you can put in a portfolio.

The mindset shift: a dashboard is not a pile of charts, it is an answer to a question a specific person asks every Monday. Everything you build this week serves that one idea, and weeks 2 onward extend this same Superstore report rather than starting over.

items.title: Git, version control from day 1
items.body:
## The one picture that prevents 90% of Git confusion

Git keeps your work in three places, and almost every beginner mistake comes from not knowing which one you are touching:

- **Working directory** is the files on your computer right now, exactly as you are editing them.
- **Staging area** is a holding tray for the precise changes you want in your next snapshot.
- **History** is the permanent timeline of snapshots you have already saved.

A **commit** moves changes from the staging area into history. A **push** copies that history up to GitHub so it lives somewhere other than your laptop. Every command below is just moving your work between these places. Hold this picture in your head and the commands stop feeling random.

## What Git is and why every team uses it

Git is the version-control tool behind essentially every codebase past day one. It snapshots your project after each meaningful change so you can see exactly what changed, undo a mistake without losing everything else, and work alongside other people without overwriting each other. You will use it every single day on this track, and the handful of commands below cover about 95% of daily work.

## Install Git and tell it who you are

```bash
# macOS:   brew install git
# Windows: winget install Git.Git   (or download from git-scm.com)
# Linux:   sudo apt install git

git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

`git --version` prints something like `git version 2.43.0`. If you instead see `command not found`, Git is not installed yet. Install it, then reopen your terminal so the new program is found.

The two `config` lines touch no project at all. They write your identity into a settings file in your home folder so every future commit is stamped with who made it. Skip them and your very first commit dies with `Author identity unknown`.

## The five commands you will actually use

```bash
git init               # turn the current folder into a Git repo
git status             # what has changed since the last commit?
git add file.py        # move one change into the staging area
git commit -m "msg"    # save everything staged as one snapshot
git log --oneline      # the list of snapshots, newest first
```

Walk them in the order you would really use them:

- `git init` creates a hidden `.git` folder, and that folder *is* the repo. You run it once per project. It prints `Initialized empty Git repository`.
- `git status` is the command you will run most. It shows which files changed and whether they are staged yet. Run it whenever you are unsure what state you are in, because it never changes anything itself.
- `git add file.py` moves that file's changes into staging. Nothing is saved yet, you are only choosing what goes into the next snapshot. Use `git add .` to stage everything at once.
- `git commit -m "msg"` writes everything staged into history as one snapshot. The `-m` flag is your one-line note to your future self about what changed. It prints something like `1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)`.
- `git log --oneline` prints one short line per commit so you can read the trail of your work. Press `q` to leave the log view.

## Push it to GitHub so it survives your laptop

```bash
# after creating an empty repo on github.com:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/your-repo.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

- `git remote add origin ...` saves GitHub's URL under the nickname `origin`. From here on, `origin` simply means "the GitHub copy."
- `git branch -M main` renames your current branch to `main` so it matches what GitHub expects.
- `git push -u origin main` uploads your commits to GitHub. The `-u` flag links your local `main` to GitHub's copy so that next time you can just type `git push`. Refresh the GitHub page and your files are there.

## When it breaks, and it will

- `Author identity unknown` means you skipped the two `git config` lines above. Run them, then commit again.
- `fatal: not a git repository` means you are not inside a repo folder. `cd` into the project, or run `git init` first.
- `failed to push some refs` means GitHub has a commit your laptop does not. Run `git pull` to merge it down, then push again.
- `nothing to commit, working tree clean` is not an error. Git is telling you there are no staged changes to save right now.

## Where Git shows up next

Every project on this track ships to GitHub, and every check-in you submit is backed by a commit. This is a prerequisite for everything that follows. Read it once now, and come back to it any time you are unsure which of the three places your work is currently sitting in.

## What it is
BI work happens in two tools you'll touch every week:
1. **Excel**, for quick analysis, ad-hoc pivots, the universal 'send me the file' format.
2. **Power BI Desktop**, Microsoft's free dashboard builder. Where serious BI work lives.

By the end of today you have both, and you've loaded a CSV into Power BI Desktop and made one chart.

## What you'll do today
Install Excel (Microsoft 365 trial if you don't already have it). Install Power BI Desktop (free) from powerbi.microsoft.com. Download a sample CSV, load it into Power BI, drag two fields onto the canvas, see a chart appear.

items.title: What is Power BI?
items.body:
## Power BI: the tool the job asks for by name

Open almost any BI analyst posting and "Power BI" sits in the requirements, usually right next to SQL and Excel. It is Microsoft's analytics tool, and because most companies already run Microsoft 365, it is the default in finance, retail, healthcare, and government. Learn it well and you clear the first filter on a large share of BI roles.

## Three tools in one app

Power BI looks like one program, but it is really three stages stitched together, and the whole game is understanding the split:

- **Power Query** cleans and reshapes the raw data. This is the ETL step: rename columns, fix types, drop junk rows, all before a single chart exists.
- **The data model** links your tables with relationships, a sales table joined to a date table joined to a product table. This is the "star schema" you build on Day 4.
- **DAX** is the formula language. DAX *measures* turn the modelled tables into the numbers a business asks for: total sales, profit margin, sales versus last year.

Everything then feeds the **report canvas**, where you lay out visuals and publish to a live URL.

## The mindset shift

A dashboard is not a pile of pretty charts. It is a question-answering machine for one audience. Before building anything, ask: who reads this, and what decision do they make from it? A regional sales manager asks "which region is behind target, and why?" The dashboard exists to answer that in five seconds, not to display every column in the data.

## This week

You will build the full pipeline on the **Sample Superstore** dataset (a classic retail-orders file): install Power BI, clean it in Power Query, model it, write six DAX measures, lay out one dashboard page, and publish it with a real link for your portfolio. Today is orientation. Watch a short Power BI overview, then write one sentence naming the audience for your Superstore dashboard and the single question it will answer. That sentence is your compass for the rest of the week.

items.title: Install Power BI Desktop
items.body:
## Install Power BI Desktop (it is free)

Power BI Desktop is the free Windows application where you build everything this week. Do not confuse it with the paid Power BI *Pro* licence, that is only for sharing in the cloud, and you do not need it to learn.

**Install it.** Easiest route: open the Microsoft Store, search "Power BI Desktop", and install. It then auto-updates monthly. Alternative: go to powerbi.microsoft.com, choose Download > Power BI Desktop, and run the installer. Either way, launch it and you should see a welcome screen with a blank report canvas, a ribbon across the top, and three icons down the left edge (Report, Data, Model). Those three icons are the three tools from yesterday.

**On a Mac?** Power BI Desktop is Windows-only, this trips people up constantly. Your zero-cost options: run Windows in a free virtual machine (VirtualBox), use a Windows PC you can access, or do the modelling exercises in the web-based Power BI Service (more limited, but enough to follow along). Pick one now so you are not blocked on Day 3.

**Load the data.** Download the Sample Superstore CSV (linked in the Day 7 dataset card, or search "Sample Superstore csv"). In Power BI: **Home > Get Data > Text/CSV**, select the file, and the Navigator window previews the table. Click **Transform Data**, not Load, because you always clean before you load. That drops you into Power Query, which is tomorrow.

**Common snag:** if numbers show as text (left-aligned) or dates look wrong, do not fix them on the canvas. Every fix belongs in Power Query, where it is recorded and repeats on refresh. Loading dirty data and patching it later is the number-one beginner mistake.

days.title: Clean in Power Query
days.summary: Today we clean the data BEFORE we model.

items.title: Clean in Power Query
items.body:
## Clean in Power Query, before you model

The rule that separates analysts from spreadsheet-pokers: **clean the data before you model it**, and do every fix in Power Query so it is recorded and repeatable. Power Query writes down each step you take, so when next month's file arrives, you click Refresh and the entire clean-up runs again automatically. That is the magic, you clean once, not every month.

You are already in the Power Query Editor from yesterday (Transform Data). On the right, the **Applied Steps** panel is your recorded recipe. Work through the Superstore table:

1. **Set data types.** Click each column header's type icon: Order Date and Ship Date to Date, Sales and Profit to Decimal Number, Quantity to Whole Number, Postal Code to Text (so leading zeros survive). Wrong types break everything downstream.
2. **Check for errors and nulls.** Select all columns, then **Home > Remove Rows > Remove Errors**. Use the column header dropdowns to scan for blanks in key fields.
3. **Trim and clean text.** Select text columns, **Transform > Format > Trim** and **Clean**, to kill stray spaces and hidden characters that split "West " and "West" into two regions.
4. **Drop what you do not need.** Right-click any column you will never analyse (e.g. Row ID) and Remove. A lean model is a fast model.

When it looks right, **Home > Close & Apply**. Power BI loads the cleaned table.

**Failure mode:** you "fix" a value by hand in a cell. Power Query is not a spreadsheet, there is no by-hand cell editing, and that is intentional. If a value is wrong, you transform the *rule* (replace values, filter, change type) so the fix survives the next refresh.

days.title: Build a date dimension table
days.summary: BI works best with a separate calendar table. Today we make one.

items.title: Build a date dimension table
items.body:
## Build a date dimension (a separate calendar table)

Time questions, "sales this month versus last", "year-to-date profit", are the bread and butter of BI, and they need a dedicated **date table**. Your Orders table cannot do it alone: it only has dates where orders happened, so it has gaps (no orders on a holiday = a missing day), and DAX time intelligence needs a *continuous* calendar with every date in range.

**Make one with DAX.** On the **Modeling** tab, choose **New Table**, and enter:

```
Date = CALENDAR(DATE(2014,1,1), DATE(2018,12,31))
```

Use the real min and max of your Order Date. This creates a row for every single day. Now add helper columns with **New Column**, for example:

```
Year = YEAR('Date'[Date])
Month = FORMAT('Date'[Date], "mmm")
MonthNo = MONTH('Date'[Date])
```

**Two steps people forget, and then their charts look broken:**
- **Sort Month by MonthNo.** Select the Month column, **Column tools > Sort by column > MonthNo**, or your months sort alphabetically (Apr, Aug, Dec...) instead of calendar order.
- **Mark as a date table.** Select the table, **Table tools > Mark as date table**, pick the Date column. This unlocks time intelligence.

**Relate it.** Switch to the **Model** view (left icon). Drag `Date[Date]` onto `Orders[Order Date]`. You now have a one-to-many relationship: the calendar table on the "one" side, orders on the "many". This little join is the start of your **star schema**, a central facts table (Orders) surrounded by dimension tables (Date, and later Product, Customer). Get this shape right and DAX becomes easy; get it wrong and every measure fights you.

days.title: Write 6 DAX measures
days.summary: DAX = the formula language of Power BI. Today: 6 measures.

items.title: Write 6 DAX measures
items.body:
## Write 6 DAX measures

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language that turns your modelled tables into the actual numbers. The single most important concept: a **measure** is not a column. A column is computed once per row and stored. A measure is computed *on the fly, in the current filter context*, so the same `Total Sales` measure shows the grand total on a card, the per-region total in a bar chart, and the per-month total in a line chart, automatically. Reach for measures, not columns, for anything you aggregate.

Create one with **Modeling > New Measure**. Write these six:

```
Total Sales = SUM(Orders[Sales])
Total Profit = SUM(Orders[Profit])
Order Count = DISTINCTCOUNT(Orders[Order ID])
Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
Sales YoY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
```

A few things worth internalising as you type them:
- **Reuse measures inside measures.** `Profit Margin` calls `[Total Sales]`, it does not re-`SUM`. Build small measures and compose them.
- **Always use `DIVIDE`, never `/`.** `DIVIDE` returns a clean blank instead of an `Infinity` error when the denominator is zero. That one habit prevents ugly dashboards.
- **`CALCULATE` is the heart of DAX.** It changes the filter context of a calculation. `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` only works because you marked the date table yesterday.

Format them now (Measure tools > Format): currency for Sales and Profit, percentage for Margin and YoY. **Failure mode:** putting the raw `Sales` *field* on a card instead of the `Total Sales` *measure*, it may look the same on one card but breaks the moment you add a filter. Build the measure, use the measure.

days.summary: Today you arrange everything into a 1-page dashboard.

items.title: Build the dashboard page
items.body:
## Build the dashboard page

Now you turn measures into a one-page answer for the audience you named on Day 1. Switch to **Report** view. The goal is not "use every chart Power BI offers", it is to answer the question fast.

A clean, standard layout that works for almost any sales dashboard:
- **KPI cards across the top:** drag `Total Sales`, `Total Profit`, `Profit Margin`, `Order Count` each onto a **Card** visual. These are the headline numbers a manager reads first.
- **A trend, top-middle:** a **Line chart** with `Date[Month]` on the axis and `Total Sales` (and `Sales LY` as a second line) shows momentum over time.
- **A breakdown, left:** a **Bar chart** of `Total Sales` by `Region` (or Category), sorted descending, so the biggest contributors jump out.
- **Detail, bottom:** a **Table** or **Matrix** of `Sub-Category` with Sales, Profit, and Margin for the people who want the numbers.

Then make it interactive: add a **Slicer** for Year and one for Region. Clicking a slicer filters every visual at once, that cross-filtering is what makes a dashboard feel alive versus a static report.

**Layout principles that read as professional:** most important thing top-left (people read in a Z), consistent colours (pick two or three, not a rainbow), clear titles on every visual, and white space, do not cram. **Failure mode:** the "wall of charts" where ten visuals fight for attention and answer nothing. If a visual does not help answer your Day 1 question, cut it. A focused four-visual page beats a cluttered twelve-visual one every time.

items.title: Publish + share + GitHub
items.body:
## Publish, share, and put it in your portfolio

A dashboard that lives only on your laptop is not a portfolio piece. Today it gets a real, shareable URL.

**Publish to the Power BI Service (free).** Click **Home > Publish**. Sign in with a Microsoft account (a free work or school account works; personal Outlook accounts sometimes cannot publish, if so, sign up for a free Microsoft 365 Developer account or use a school email). Choose **My workspace**. After a moment you get a "Success" dialog with an **Open in Power BI** link. Click it and your dashboard is now running in the browser at a real URL.

**A note on sharing on the free tier:** sharing a report *with other people* through the Service technically needs a Pro licence on both ends. For a portfolio, you do not need that. What you do instead:
- Take a clean **screenshot** (or a short screen recording) of the live dashboard.
- Use **File > Export > Export to PDF** for a shareable static version.
- Note the live URL for interviews where you can screen-share.

**Put it on GitHub.** Create a repo named `superstore-bi`. Add the `.pbix` file, a clear **README** (what the dashboard answers, the data source, the six measures, a sentence on what you learned), and the **screenshot** embedded at the top. Because `.pbix` is a binary file GitHub will not preview, the README and screenshot are what actually sell it, write them for a hiring manager who will not open Power BI.

That repo is portfolio artefact number one for this track: a real, published BI dashboard, built end to end from raw CSV to live URL, with the pipeline (clean, model, measure, visualise, publish) you will repeat in every BI job.

weeks.title: Superstore BI v0.2: Drillthrough + tooltips
weeks.context:
Drillthrough is one of the most powerful features in Power BI and Tableau, it lets a user click on a data point and navigate to a detail page scoped to exactly that item. Instead of building 10 separate reports for 10 regions, you build one drillthrough page and every region gets its own contextual detail view.

Tooltips extend the base visualisation by showing additional information when a user hovers over a data point, without cluttering the main chart. Used well, they surface secondary metrics (like profit margin when hovering over a sales bar) that would otherwise need a separate chart.

This week you build these features in Power BI Desktop (free) using the Superstore dataset. The underlying skill being practised is information hierarchy: what is the primary view, what is the detail, and when should each be shown.

items.title: What's drillthrough?
items.body:
## Drillthrough: one detail page instead of ten reports

Last week you shipped a one-page Superstore dashboard. This week you make it *interactive* like a real product. Drillthrough is the first power feature: a user right-clicks a data point, say the "West" bar, and jumps to a detail page already filtered to West. One page serves every region, every category, every customer.

The alternative, which beginners build and then regret, is ten near-identical pages (West Detail, East Detail, ...) that all break the moment the business adds a region. Drillthrough replaces all of them with a single template page that receives whatever the user clicked.

## How it works, conceptually

You build one **detail page**, tell Power BI which field it "drills through on" (e.g. Region), and Power BI does the rest: when a user drills through from any visual filtered by Region, it opens your detail page with that region's filter already applied. The page is a template; the filter is the input.

Today is orientation: open last week's report, decide what a manager would want to see *after* clicking a region (its top products, its monthly trend, its profit by segment), and sketch that detail page on paper. The rest of the week builds it. By Friday you republish as Superstore BI v0.2 with working drillthrough and custom tooltips, the kind of polish that makes a dashboard feel professional rather than student-made.

items.title: Build the Region Detail page
items.body:
## Build the Region Detail page

Add a new page (the **+** at the bottom) and name it `Region Detail`. This is the template that every region will reuse, so build it to answer "tell me everything about this one region".

A solid detail layout:
- A **title** that will show the region name (you will make it dynamic later, for now just "Region Detail").
- KPI **cards**: `Total Sales`, `Total Profit`, `Profit Margin` (your measures from Week 1).
- A **bar chart**: Sales by Sub-Category, sorted descending, the region's product mix.
- A **line chart**: Sales by Month, the region's trend.
- A **table**: top customers by Sales.

Build it with the page *unfiltered* for now, so you see all-region numbers while you design. That is expected, the per-region filter only arrives when a user actually drills through.

**Make the title dynamic (the touch that impresses):** create a measure like

```
Region Title = "Detail: " & SELECTEDVALUE(Orders[Region], "All Regions")
```

and drop it into a Card or a Text box. `SELECTEDVALUE` returns the single region in context, or the fallback when none is selected. When a user drills through to West, the title reads "Detail: West" automatically. Small thing, big "this person knows the tool" signal.

items.title: Enable drillthrough
items.body:
## Enable drillthrough

Now wire it up. On the `Region Detail` page, open the **Visualizations** pane and find the **Drill through** well at the bottom. Drag `Orders[Region]` into the **Add drill-through fields here** box.

That one action does something subtle but important: Power BI automatically adds a **back button** (top-left) to the detail page, and it makes "Drill through > Region Detail" appear in the right-click menu of any visual on other pages that is filtered by Region.

**Test it.** Go to your main dashboard page, right-click the West bar in your Sales-by-Region chart, and choose **Drill through > Region Detail**. The detail page opens, every visual now scoped to West, and your dynamic title reads "Detail: West". Click the back button to return. That is the whole feature working.

**The failure mode to recognise:** drillthrough only appears in the right-click menu when the visual you click is actually filtered by the drillthrough field. If "Drill through" is greyed out, the visual you right-clicked does not have Region in its filter context, click a visual that breaks data down by Region. This confuses everyone the first time; now you will know what it means.

items.title: Custom tooltips
items.body:
## Custom tooltips: a mini-report on hover

Default tooltips show one number when you hover a data point. A **custom tooltip** shows a whole mini-report, a tiny page that pops up on hover, scoped to whatever you are hovering. It is the detail-on-demand that makes a dashboard feel rich without cluttering the main view.

**Build one.** Add a new page, name it `Tooltip - Region`, and in **Page information** set **Allow use as tooltip = On** and set the page **Canvas size** to **Tooltip** (small). On this little page, add two or three compact visuals: a card for Total Sales and a small bar of Sales by Category.

**Attach it.** Go back to your main Sales-by-Region bar chart, open its **Format > Tooltip** settings, set type to **Report page**, and pick `Tooltip - Region`. Now hover any region bar: your mini-report appears, filtered to that region.

This is the same filter-context idea as drillthrough, just triggered by hover instead of click, and it is one of the features that separates a polished BI report from a wall of static charts. Use it sparingly: one well-made tooltip on the most-examined visual beats tooltips on everything.

items.title: Bookmarks for views
items.body:
## Bookmarks: save and switch views

A **bookmark** captures the current state of a page, which visuals are visible, what filters and slicers are set, and lets a user jump back to it with one click. Two everyday uses:

- **Saved views.** Capture "This Year vs Last Year" and "By Category" as two bookmarks, then add buttons so a manager toggles between them without touching a slicer.
- **Show/hide panels.** Build a filter panel that slides in and out, a common polished-dashboard trick, by bookmarking the panel visible and hidden and wiring buttons to each.

**Do it:** set your slicers/visuals the way you want view one, then **View > Bookmarks > Add**. Rename it. Change the state, add a second bookmark. Then add **Insert > Buttons**, and in each button's **Action**, set Type = Bookmark and pick the bookmark. Use the **Selection** pane (View > Selection) to show or hide specific visuals inside a bookmark.

**Gotcha:** by default a bookmark saves *Data, Display, and Current page*. If you only want it to switch which visuals show (not reset filters), open the bookmark's "..." menu and untick **Data**. Forgetting this is why bookmarks sometimes "reset everything" unexpectedly.

items.title: Tag v0.2

## Tag v0.2

You version your BI work the same way developers version code, so you can show progress and roll back if needed. Today you mark this milestone.

In your `superstore-bi` GitHub repo: commit the updated `.pbix`, update the README to describe the new capabilities (drillthrough detail page, custom tooltips, bookmark views), and refresh the screenshot. Then create a release/tag named `v0.2`.

```
git add . && git commit -m "Superstore BI v0.2: drillthrough + tooltips + bookmarks"

Why bother tagging a dashboard? It also means each week's milestone is a clean, named point you can point to.

Write one line in your README on what v0.2 added and why it matters to a user (drillthrough = one page serves every region; tooltips = detail without clutter). That framing, feature tied to user value, is exactly how you will talk about your work on the job.

weeks.title: Superstore BI v0.3: Row-level security
weeks.context:
Row-level security (RLS) is what makes a BI report multi-tenant, the same report shows different data to different users based on their identity. A regional sales manager sees only their region. A product manager sees only their product category. The CEO sees everything.

Without RLS, sharing a Power BI report means sharing all the data in it. With RLS, you can publish one report to an entire organisation and each person sees only what they are authorised to see. This is not optional in enterprise BI, it is required any time data access needs to be restricted by role.

This week you implement RLS in Power BI Desktop using static roles, then learn how dynamic RLS works using USERPRINCIPALNAME(), the function that returns the logged-in user's email address and enables automatic filtering based on identity.

items.title: What is RLS?
items.body:
## Row-level security: one report, different data per person

Row-level security (RLS) is what makes a single report multi-tenant: the same dashboard shows different rows to different people based on who they are. The West manager opens it and sees only West. The East manager sees only East. The CEO sees everything. One report, one URL, but the data is scoped to the viewer.

Without RLS, companies do the painful thing: build and email separate filtered files to each manager, which is slow, leaks easily, and goes stale instantly. RLS replaces all of that with rules enforced by Power BI itself, a manager literally cannot see another region's numbers, even if they fiddle with filters.

## How it works

You define **roles** (e.g. "West Manager") and give each role a **DAX filter** on a table (e.g. `Orders[Region] = "West"`). Then you assign real people to roles in the Power BI Service. When someone opens the report, Power BI silently applies their role's filter to every query, so every visual, measure, and export respects it.

This week you add RLS to your Superstore report and ship v0.3. Today, orient: list the audiences (regional managers, a CEO who sees all) and the filter rule each needs. Security is a feature you design before you build, so this planning is the work, not a warm-up.

items.title: Create roles
items.body:
## Create roles

In Power BI Desktop, open **Modeling > Manage roles** (newer versions: the security icon). This is where roles live.

Create a role per region. For a quick approach, one role with a dynamic rule is cleaner than five hard-coded ones, but start by understanding the explicit version:

- **Manage roles > Create**, name it `West`, select the `Orders` table, and enter the DAX filter:
```
[Region] = "West"
```
- Repeat for `East`, `Central`, `South`.

Each role now means "a person in this role only sees rows where the filter is true". The filter is plain DAX returning true/false per row.

**The better, scalable pattern (worth knowing now):** instead of one role per region, use a single dynamic role driven by the logged-in user. If you had a security table mapping user emails to regions, the filter becomes:
```
[Region] = LOOKUPVALUE(Security[Region], Security[Email], USERPRINCIPALNAME())
```
`USERPRINCIPALNAME()` returns the email of whoever is viewing. One role then serves everyone, and you manage access by editing a table, not by adding roles. For Superstore you will use the explicit roles (no user table), but in a real job the dynamic pattern is what scales.

items.title: Test as a role
items.body:
## Test as a role (before anyone else does)

Never ship security you have not tested. Power BI Desktop lets you impersonate a role and see exactly what that person would see.

**Modeling > View as** (or the "View as roles" button). Tick `West` and click OK. A banner appears across the top: "Now viewing as: West". Every visual on every page instantly reflects only West data, your KPI cards drop to West's totals, the region bar chart shows only West, the map zooms to West.

Click through your pages and confirm:
- No East/Central/South data leaks anywhere, including in tooltips and the drillthrough detail page from last week.
- Totals make sense (West's Total Sales is less than the all-region total you saw before).

Then **View as > None** to return to full view, and test another role.

**The failure mode RLS beginners hit:** a measure or visual that bypasses the filtered table still shows everything. RLS filters the table you wrote the rule on (`Orders`); if some visual is built on a different, unfiltered table, it leaks. Testing every page as every role is how you catch this. Security you assume works is security that does not, verify by impersonation, every time.

items.title: Add an 'All Regions' role for CEO
items.body:
## Add an "All Regions" role for the CEO

Managers see their slice; leadership sees everything. You need a role that applies no row filter, so its members see all data.

In **Manage roles**, create a role named `All Regions` (or `Leadership`). Select the `Orders` table but leave the filter blank, or, more explicitly and self-documenting, enter:
```
TRUE()
```
A filter of `TRUE()` is true for every row, so the role sees everything. An empty filter does the same, but writing `TRUE()` makes the intent obvious to the next analyst who opens your file: "this role is deliberately unrestricted", not "someone forgot to add a filter".

**Test it:** View as `All Regions`, confirm you see full company numbers, the same as no role at all.

A subtlety worth knowing: if a person is assigned to *multiple* roles, Power BI shows the **union** of what those roles allow (the filters are OR-ed). So you would not assign the CEO to both `West` and `All Regions`, just `All Regions`. Assigning someone to a broad role and a narrow role gives them the broad access. Keep role assignment clean: each person in exactly the role that matches their access.

items.title: Republish + assign
items.body:
## Republish and assign people to roles

Defining roles in Desktop is only half of RLS, the actual assignment of *people* happens in the Power BI Service after you publish.

**Publish** the report (overwrite the existing one). Then in the Service, go to your workspace, find the **dataset/semantic model** (not the report), open its **More options (...) > Security**. You will see your roles listed (West, East, ..., All Regions). For each role, add the email addresses of the people who belong to it. Click Save.

Now when those users open the report, their role's filter applies automatically. They cannot remove it, it is enforced server-side, not in the visuals.

**Reality check on licensing:** assigning and sharing RLS reports to other people uses Power BI Pro. For learning and your portfolio you do not need to actually invite colleagues, the roles, the DAX filters, and the "View as" tests are the skill, and they all work on the free Desktop. In an interview you explain: "I defined these roles, here's the dynamic USERPRINCIPALNAME pattern for scale, and assignment happens in the Service Security panel." That demonstrates the competence without needing a paid tenant.

Security that only you understand is a liability. Before tagging v0.3, write a short **security model** doc (a page in your README or a separate `SECURITY.md`):

weeks.title: Superstore BI v0.4: Refresh + data gateway
weeks.context:
A dashboard that doesn't refresh is a snapshot, not a BI tool. Data refresh is what makes Power BI a living reporting system, reports update automatically as the underlying data changes, without anyone manually re-uploading a file.

Power BI has two refresh paths: cloud data sources (SQL databases in Azure, BigQuery, Snowflake) refresh directly from the Service with stored credentials. On-premise data sources (a local SQL Server, an Excel file on a company network drive) require a Power BI Gateway, software installed on a machine in the corporate network that acts as a secure bridge between Power BI Service in the cloud and data sources on-premise.

This week you configure scheduled refresh in the Power BI Service and understand the gateway architecture. You also learn incremental refresh, the pattern that refreshes only new/changed data instead of reloading the entire dataset, which is critical for large data sources.

items.title: Why automatic refresh
items.body:
## Why automatic refresh turns a file into a system

A dashboard that does not refresh is a snapshot. You built it on Monday's data, and by Friday it quietly lies. The thing that turns Power BI from "a fancy screenshot" into a living BI system is **scheduled refresh**: the report pulls the latest data on its own, on a timetable, with nobody re-uploading anything.

This is the difference a business actually pays for. A static report needs an analyst to manually rebuild it every week (and they forget, and it drifts). A refreshing report is just *true* every morning. When a manager asks "is this current?", the answer is "yes, it refreshed at 6am", not "let me redo it".

## The two refresh architectures

- **Cloud source (easy path):** if your data lives somewhere the Power BI Service can reach directly, OneDrive/SharePoint, a cloud database, an API, the Service refreshes it by itself. No extra software.
- **On-premises source (gateway path):** if your data lives on a company server or a local file on someone's PC, you install a **data gateway**, a small bridge program that lets the cloud Service reach the on-prem data securely.

This week you take the easy path: move the Superstore file to OneDrive so the Service can refresh it directly, then schedule it. You will understand the gateway concept (interviewers ask about it) without needing a server. Ship target: Superstore BI v0.4, a report that updates itself.

items.title: Move the file to OneDrive
items.body:
## Move the file to OneDrive

Right now your report reads `superstore.csv` from a folder on your laptop. The Power BI Service in the cloud cannot see your laptop, so it could never refresh from there. The fix: put the file somewhere the cloud can reach. OneDrive (or SharePoint) is the simplest.

**Steps:**
1. Sign in to OneDrive (a free Microsoft account includes it). Install the OneDrive desktop app if you want a synced local folder, or just use the web upload.
2. Create a folder like `BI-Data` in OneDrive and upload `superstore.csv` into it.
3. Confirm it is really in the cloud, open OneDrive in the browser and see the file there, not just on your disk.

Why this works: a file in OneDrive has a cloud address the Power BI Service can authenticate to and read on a schedule. A file in `C:\Users\you\Documents` does not.

**Heads up for the next step:** you are about to re-point your report from the old local path to this OneDrive copy. Keep the column names and structure identical, do not "tidy up" the file while moving it, or you will spend Day 3 fixing broken column references instead of learning refresh.

items.title: Re-point Power BI to OneDrive
items.body:
## Re-point Power BI to the OneDrive copy

Your report still references the old local file path. You need to swap the source to the OneDrive copy without rebuilding the report.

**The clean way:** open the report in Desktop, go to **Transform Data > Data source settings** (or **Home > Transform Data**, then in Power Query click the source step's gear). Change the file path from your local `C:\...\superstore.csv` to the OneDrive-synced path (if you have the OneDrive app, it is a normal folder path under your OneDrive directory; for SharePoint/OneDrive web, you use the file's web/SharePoint connector).

After changing it, **Close & Apply** and confirm every visual still shows data. Because the file's structure is unchanged, all your Power Query steps, the model, the measures, the visuals, just re-run against the new location. Nothing else should move.

**The failure mode here is real and common:** if column names differ even slightly between the old and new file, Power Query throws errors like *"Column 'Sales' of the table wasn't found"* and visuals go blank. That is why Day 2 said do not edit the file while moving it. If you hit this, open Power Query, find the red error step, and fix the column reference, do not delete and rebuild. Source-swapping is a routine job in real BI (files move, databases migrate); doing it without rebuilding is the skill.

items.title: Simulate an update
items.body:
## Simulate an update

A refreshing report is only believable if you watch it actually change. So simulate new data landing.

1. Open the `superstore.csv` in OneDrive (download, edit, re-upload, or edit in Excel online). Add a few new rows, say, a handful of new orders dated this month, with real-looking Sales and Profit, or bump an existing region's sales.
2. Save / re-upload so the OneDrive copy now contains the change.
3. In the Service, trigger **Refresh now** on the dataset (or wait for the schedule).
4. Open the report and confirm the numbers moved: your Total Sales card is higher, the new month appears on the trend line.

That round trip, edit the source, refresh, see the dashboard update, is the entire value proposition of BI made concrete. In production the "edit the file" step is really "the sales system wrote new orders to the database overnight", but the mechanism is identical: source changes, scheduled refresh runs, dashboard is current by morning.

**What you have proven:** your report is no longer a thing you maintain by hand. It maintains itself. That is the line between a spreadsheet jockey and a BI analyst who builds systems.

items.title: Add a 'Last refreshed' indicator
items.body:
## Add a "Last refreshed" indicator

Users trust a dashboard more when it tells them how fresh it is. A "Last refreshed: 12 Oct, 6:02am" stamp answers the silent question every viewer has, "am I looking at current data?", before they have to ask.

Power BI does not expose the refresh time as a normal field, so you create it during refresh with a tiny Power Query step:

1. In Power Query, **New Source > Blank Query**, and in the formula bar enter:
```
= DateTime.LocalNow()
```
2. Right-click the result > **To Table**, rename the column `LastRefresh`, set its type to Date/Time, and rename the query `RefreshInfo`. **Close & Apply.**
3. Create a measure:
```
Last Refreshed = "Last refreshed: " & FORMAT(MAX(RefreshInfo[LastRefresh]), "dd mmm yyyy, hh:mm")
```
4. Drop it into a **Card** or text box in a corner of your dashboard.

Because `DateTime.LocalNow()` is evaluated *each time the dataset refreshes*, the stamp updates automatically to the moment of the last refresh. (One nuance: it reflects the refresh time in the Service's processing context; for a portfolio that is exactly right.) Small feature, big trust signal, and it shows you think about the user's experience, not just the numbers.

weeks.title: Superstore BI v0.5: Model & DAX foundations
weeks.context:
You have shipped four versions of the Superstore report, published dashboard, drillthrough, row-level security, scheduled refresh. It looks finished. It is not. Under every report that gets a number wrong is the same root cause: the model layer was never understood, only assembled by trial and error.

This week you stop adding features and go down a layer. Power BI has three layers: data (Power Query, clean and shape), model (tables, relationships, measures), and report (visuals). Most analysts live only in the report layer and patch wrong numbers with filters and hacks. You are going to own the model layer of the Superstore file you already have.

The single concept that separates people who can build dashboards from people who can be trusted with them is filter context: a measure is not a stored value, it is a formula that recomputes against whatever filters surround it. CALCULATE is the function that lets you change those filters on purpose. By Friday you will be able to look at any wrong number in your own report and know which layer broke it.

items.title: Measures vs calculated columns
items.body:
## Measures vs calculated columns: the choice that decides everything

You have shipped four versions of Superstore. It looks finished. It is not, because most reports that quietly show a *wrong* number trace back to one root cause: the author did not understand the model layer, and reached for a calculated column when they needed a measure, or vice versa. This week you make the model bulletproof.

The single most important distinction in Power BI:

- A **calculated column** is computed **once per row, at refresh, and stored** in the table. It has a *row context*: it knows "this row". Use it when each row needs a value that depends only on that row, e.g. `Profit per Unit = Orders[Profit] / Orders[Quantity]`, or a category bucket you will slice by.
- A **measure** is computed **on the fly, at query time, in the current filter context**. It does not store anything. Use it for anything you **aggregate**, totals, averages, ratios, because the same measure re-evaluates correctly at every level: grand total on a card, per-region in a bar, per-month in a line.

The rule of thumb: **if you will aggregate it, make it a measure; if you will slice or filter by it, make it a column.** Beginners default to columns because they feel like Excel. That bloats the model and produces totals that do not add up (a column of ratios summed gives nonsense). Reach for measures first.

Today, audit your Superstore file: list every calculated column and measure you have, and for each ask "is this the right type?" You will likely find a column that should have been a measure. Fixing that mindset is the work of the week.

items.title: Audit your star schema
items.body:
## Audit your star schema

A **star schema** is the shape every good Power BI model takes: one central **fact** table (the events, your `Orders`) surrounded by **dimension** tables (the descriptors, `Date`, and ideally `Product`, `Customer`, `Region`). Relationships flow one-to-many from each dimension into the fact. Get this shape and DAX is easy and filters flow correctly; flatten everything into one wide table and you fight the tool forever.

Open the **Model** view and look at your Superstore model honestly. Right now you probably have `Orders` plus the `Date` table you built in Week 1. That is a minimal star. Strengthen it:

- **Confirm the Date relationship** is one-to-many (Date one side, Orders many side), single-direction, on `Date[Date]` -> `Orders[Order Date]`.
- **Consider splitting out dimensions.** Product fields (Category, Sub-Category, Product Name) repeat across thousands of order rows. In a mature model they live in a `Product` dimension joined to Orders. For Superstore you can leave them on the fact for now, but understand *why* a real model separates them: smaller fact table, single place to fix a product name, cleaner slicers.
- **Check relationship direction.** Filters flow *from* the "one" side (dimension) *to* the "many" side (fact). If a slicer is not filtering a visual, a wrong or missing relationship is the usual cause.

Draw your current star on paper, fact in the middle, dimensions around it, arrows showing filter direction. If it does not look like a star, it is the source of future wrong numbers.

items.title: Filter context, felt, not memorised
items.body:
## Filter context, felt, not memorised

Filter context is the one DAX concept that, once it clicks, makes everything else obvious, and until it clicks, makes DAX feel like guessing. Here is the felt version.

**Every cell in a Power BI visual is a question with filters attached.** When `Total Sales` shows 90,000 on a card with no filters, it summed every row. When the same measure shows 23,000 in the "West" row of a bar chart, the bar *added the filter Region = West* before the measure ran. You did not write that filter; the visual did, by virtue of where the number sits.

So a measure does not have one value, it has a value *per context*. `Total Sales = SUM(Orders[Sales])` means "sum Sales, of whatever rows are currently in context". The card, the bar, the matrix cell each create a different context, and the same measure answers each correctly. That is why measures beat columns for aggregation.

**Feel it directly:** put `Total Sales` on a card (grand total), then in a matrix with Region on rows (per-region), then add Year to columns (per region-and-year). Same measure, three different numbers, because three different filter contexts. Now add a slicer and click it: every number recomputes, because the slicer added another filter to every context.

Internalise this sentence: *a measure is evaluated in the filter context of where it appears.* Tomorrow you learn the function that lets you **change** that context on purpose, which is where DAX becomes powerful.

items.title: CALCULATE, overriding filters
items.body:
## CALCULATE: overriding the filter context

`CALCULATE` is the most important function in DAX. It does one thing: it **changes the filter context** of a calculation. Almost every non-trivial business measure is a `CALCULATE`.

Syntax: `CALCULATE( <expression>, <filter1>, <filter2>, ... )`. It evaluates the expression, but first it applies (adds or replaces) the filters you give it.

Concrete examples on Superstore:

```
Sales West = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Orders[Region] = "West")
```
This ignores the visual's region context and forces West, useful for a "West vs total" comparison.

```
Pct of Total = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Orders)))
```
`ALL(Orders)` **removes** filters, so the denominator is the grand total regardless of the current row. Now each region's bar can show its % of company sales, a classic, and impossible without CALCULATE.

```
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
```
The time-intelligence measure from Week 1 is a CALCULATE that shifts the date filter back a year.

The mental model: a measure *reads* the current filter context; `CALCULATE` *rewrites* it for the duration of one calculation. `ALL` removes filters, an explicit condition replaces them, time functions shift them. Once you see every advanced measure as "CALCULATE plus a context change", the language stops being mysterious. Rewrite two of your existing measures using CALCULATE today to feel it.

items.title: A proper Date table + time intelligence
items.body:
## A proper Date table and time intelligence

Week 1 gave you a basic date table. Now make it production-grade, because almost every time-intelligence bug comes from a weak date table.

A proper Date table:
- **Is continuous** (every day in range, no gaps) and covers the full span of your data.
- **Is marked as a date table** (Table tools > Mark as date table). Without this, functions like `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` and `DATESYTD` misbehave or error.
- **Has the helper columns you slice by:** Year, Quarter, Month name, MonthNo (to sort), Year-Month (for a continuous axis), Day of Week. Add them as calculated columns, this is the correct use of columns: descriptors you filter and group by.
- **Is the only table your visuals use for dates.** Put `Date[Year]`/`Date[Month]` on axes and slicers, never `Orders[Order Date]` directly. That is what makes time intelligence consistent across every visual.

Now the payoff, the time-intelligence measures that interviewers expect:

```
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], 'Date'[Date])
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
Sales YoY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
Sales MTD = TOTALMTD([Total Sales], 'Date'[Date])
```

Drop `Sales YTD` and `Sales YoY %` into your dashboard. **Failure mode:** these return blank or wrong if the date table is not marked, has gaps, or you used `Orders[Order Date]` on the axis. When time intelligence "does not work", check the date table first, it is the cause nine times out of ten.

items.title: Iterators: SUMX, AVERAGEX, RANKX
items.body:
## Iterators: SUMX, AVERAGEX, RANKX

Most DAX aggregations (`SUM`, `AVERAGE`) work on a whole column. **Iterators** (the `...X` functions) are different and more powerful: they walk a table **row by row**, compute an expression in each row's context, then aggregate the results. The "X" means "expression per row".

Why you need them: when the thing you want does not exist as a column.

```
Total Revenue = SUMX(Orders, Orders[Quantity] * Orders[Unit Price])
```
There is no "revenue" column. `SUMX` multiplies quantity by price *for each order row*, then sums, no helper column needed. (Doing this as a column wastes storage; as `SUM` it is impossible because the product does not exist yet.)

```
Avg Order Value = AVERAGEX(VALUES(Orders[Order ID]), [Total Sales])
```
This averages *per order*, not per row, it iterates distinct orders and averages each order's total. A plain `AVERAGE(Sales)` would average line items, a subtly wrong number.

```
Region Rank = RANKX(ALL(Orders[Region]), [Total Sales])
```
`RANKX` ranks each region by sales, so you can show "West is #1". `ALL` gives it the full list of regions to rank against.

The pattern to recognise: **iterator = table to walk + expression to evaluate per row + aggregation.** They are how you express logic that row-level columns and simple aggregates cannot. They also cost more to compute, so prefer plain `SUM` when a column exists, and reach for `SUMX`/`AVERAGEX`/`RANKX` when it does not. Add a `Total Revenue` and a `Region Rank` to Superstore today.

weeks.title: Advanced Power BI and DAX
weeks.context:
Advanced DAX is the difference between a BI analyst who builds reports and one who builds data products. The features this week, variables, iterator functions, and advanced CALCULATE patterns, are what you need to express complex business logic that no visual configuration can handle.

Variables in DAX (VAR / RETURN) are not just a code style preference, they change evaluation. A variable captures the current filter context at the point it is declared, which prevents a common class of DAX bugs where the context changes unexpectedly inside a complex expression.

Iterator functions (SUMX, AVERAGEX, MAXX, RANKX) evaluate an expression row by row and then aggregate. They are essential when your calculation requires a per-row computation before summing, like calculating profit margin per order and then averaging those margins, rather than dividing total profit by total sales.

items.title: Time intelligence
items.body:
## Time intelligence, the advanced patterns

Beyond `TOTALYTD` and `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR`, real reporting needs rolling and comparative windows. The workhorse pattern is `CALCULATE` + `DATESINPERIOD` or `DATESBETWEEN`.

**Rolling 3-month average** (smooths noise, the most-requested trend measure):
```
Sales 3M Avg =
AVERAGEX(
  DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], MAX('Date'[Date]), -3, MONTH),
  [Total Sales]
)
```
This walks the last three months from the current point and averages them.

**Rolling 12-month total** (a moving annual total, smooths seasonality):
```
Sales R12M = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], MAX('Date'[Date]), -12, MONTH))
```

**Period-over-period generically:**
```
Sales PoP % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
```

The mental model stays constant: every time measure is `CALCULATE` (or an iterator) over a **set of dates** you construct, last 3 months, same period last year, year-to-date. Master the date-set functions (`DATESINPERIOD`, `DATESBETWEEN`, `DATESYTD`, `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR`, `PARALLELPERIOD`) and you can express any time comparison a business asks for. Add `Sales 3M Avg` to your trend line today and watch it smooth the spikes, that single measure is something managers love.

items.title: Iterator functions
items.body:
## Iterators inside CALCULATE and FILTER

You met `SUMX`/`AVERAGEX`/`RANKX` last week. Their real power shows when combined with `FILTER` inside `CALCULATE` to express conditions that simple filters cannot.

`FILTER` returns a table of rows meeting a condition; feeding it to `CALCULATE` scopes a measure to exactly those rows:

```
Sales High-Value Orders =
CALCULATE([Total Sales], FILTER(Orders, Orders[Sales] > 1000))
```
"Total sales, but only from orders over 1000." A plain filter argument cannot express `> 1000` on a measure-like condition; `FILTER` can.

Combine with iteration for genuinely advanced logic, e.g. sales from repeat customers:
```
Sales Repeat Customers =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Sales],
  FILTER(
    VALUES(Orders[Customer ID]),
    CALCULATE(DISTINCTCOUNT(Orders[Order ID])) > 1
  )
)
```
This iterates customers, keeps those with more than one order, and sums their sales. That answers a real retention question from one measure.

**The cost/benefit:** `FILTER` iterates, so it is slower than a plain `CALCULATE` filter. Rule: use a simple filter argument (`Orders[Region]="West"`) when you can; reach for `FILTER` only when the condition involves a measure or a comparison a plain filter cannot do. Knowing *when* to use the expensive tool is itself the senior skill.

days.title: Filter context vs row context
days.summary: Focus: Filter context vs row context

items.title: Filter context vs row context
items.body:
## Filter context vs row context (and context transition)

These are the two evaluation contexts in DAX, and the rule that connects them, **context transition**, is what trips up everyone who skips it.

- **Row context**: "the current row". Calculated columns and iterators (`SUMX`) have it, they know which row they are on. It does *not* automatically filter the model.
- **Filter context**: "the current set of filters". Measures run in it; it is created by visuals, slicers, and `CALCULATE`.

The crucial rule: **`CALCULATE` (including the implicit `CALCULATE` around every measure) turns the current row context into an equivalent filter context.** This is context transition. It is why, inside `SUMX(Orders, [Total Sales])`, the measure `[Total Sales]` returns the sales *of the current row's context*, not the grand total, the row context transitioned into a filter.

Concrete consequence:
```
Sales x Margin per Order = SUMX(Orders, [Total Sales] * [Profit Margin])
```
Each iteration evaluates the measures in that row's transitioned context. If you wrote a bare column expression instead, you would get different (often wrong) results.

You do not need to recite the formal definition. You need to recognise the symptom: *"my measure inside an iterator is giving per-row results, not the total"* (that is context transition working), or *"my calculated column referencing a measure shows the same value on every row"* (that is a missing/whole-table context). When DAX surprises you, ask "which context am I in, and did CALCULATE transition it?" That question resolves most confusing results.

items.title: Variables in DAX
items.body:
## Variables in DAX (VAR / RETURN)

`VAR` is the upgrade that makes complex measures readable, debuggable, and faster. A variable computes a value once, names it, and reuses it.

Compare. Without variables:
```
Sales YoY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])), CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])))
```
The last-year calculation is written twice, evaluated twice, and the whole thing is hard to read. With variables:
```
Sales YoY % =
VAR CurrentSales = [Total Sales]
VAR LastYearSales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
RETURN
DIVIDE(CurrentSales - LastYearSales, LastYearSales)
```
Clearer, computed once each, easy to change.

Three reasons to use `VAR` everywhere your measures get non-trivial:
- **Readability:** named steps tell the next analyst (and you in six months) what is happening.
- **Performance:** a variable is evaluated once and reused, not recomputed per reference.
- **Debugging:** temporarily `RETURN` a variable to inspect an intermediate value, the fastest way to find where a measure goes wrong.

One subtlety that catches people: a variable captures its value **at the point it is defined**, in that filter context. It does not "see" later `CALCULATE` context changes. Usually that is exactly what you want, but if a `VAR` seems "stuck", it is because it was evaluated before the context you expected. Rewrite three of your gnarlier Superstore measures with `VAR`/`RETURN` today; they will be shorter and clearer.

items.title: Row-level security (RLS) setup and testing
items.body:
## Dynamic row-level security with USERPRINCIPALNAME

Week 3 gave you static RLS, one role per region, hard-coded. That does not scale to 50 regions or changing staff. The production pattern is **dynamic RLS**: one role, driven by who is logged in.

The ingredients:
1. A **security table** mapping users to what they can see, e.g. `UserAccess` with columns `Email` and `Region`. (For Superstore, build a small one by hand.)
2. A relationship or lookup from that table to the data.
3. A single role whose filter uses `USERPRINCIPALNAME()`, the function that returns the email of the current viewer.

The role's DAX filter on `Orders`:
```
Orders[Region] = LOOKUPVALUE(UserAccess[Region], UserAccess[Email], USERPRINCIPALNAME())
```
Now there is **one** role. When West-manager@company logs in, `USERPRINCIPALNAME()` returns her email, `LOOKUPVALUE` finds "West", and she sees only West. Add a new manager? Add a row to the security table, no model change. Give someone two regions? The pattern extends with a relationship and `CONTAINS`/`TREATAS`.

**Test it** with **View as > Other user**, type an email from your `UserAccess` table, and confirm they see only their region. This "Other user" box is exactly how you simulate dynamic RLS in Desktop without real logins.

Dynamic RLS is a common interview topic precisely because it separates people who clicked through a tutorial from people who understand how security scales. You now have both the static and dynamic patterns, and know when each fits.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: SUM and SUMX look similar but think differently, and the gap shows up the moment your calculation needs to happen row by row. SUM(Sales[Amount]) adds an existing column, it assumes the number you want is already sitting there. SUMX is an iterator: it walks the table row by row, evaluates an expression for each row, and then totals the results. The trap is a calculation like total revenue when you only have Quantity and UnitPrice in separate columns, SUM cannot multiply them per row, so SUM(Quantity) times SUM(UnitPrice) gives a nonsense number (total quantity times total price). SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) does the multiplication on each row first, then sums, the correct answer. Show me a case where SUM gives the wrong total and SUMX fixes it, and explain exactly why the SUM version is wrong.

SQL is the lingua franca of data. Every BI tool, Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Metabase, eventually pushes a SQL query to a database. A BI analyst who cannot write SQL is dependent on an engineer to get data. A BI analyst who can write SQL gets data themselves and builds faster.

items.title: Window functions
items.body:
## Window functions: the BI analyst's superpower

A normal aggregate (`SUM`, `AVG` with `GROUP BY`) collapses many rows into one. A **window function** computes across a set of rows *but keeps every row*. That difference is why window functions power almost every interesting BI report: running totals, rankings, moving averages, "% of total", comparisons to the previous row.

The shape is always: `function() OVER (window definition)`.

```
SELECT
  order_date,
  sales,
  SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM orders;
```
`SUM(sales)` would normally need a `GROUP BY`; with `OVER (ORDER BY order_date)` it instead gives a **running total**, every row keeps its own sales *and* gains the cumulative sum up to that date. No collapsing.

The functions you will use constantly:
- **Aggregates as windows:** `SUM() OVER`, `AVG() OVER`, `COUNT() OVER`, running and moving calculations.
- **Ranking:** `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, `DENSE_RANK()`, who is 1st, 2nd, 3rd.
- **Offset:** `LAG()` and `LEAD()`, this row vs the previous/next row (month-over-month growth in one line).

```
SELECT order_date, sales,
  LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_sales,
  sales - LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS change
FROM orders;
```
That `LAG` query is period-over-period change, the SQL version of your DAX YoY measure, computed at the source. Run a running total and a `LAG` change on your `orders` table today. Once window functions click, half of "advanced SQL for analytics" is yours.

days.title: PARTITION BY and ORDER BY inside window functions
days.summary: Focus: PARTITION BY and ORDER BY inside window functions

items.title: PARTITION BY and ORDER BY inside window functions
items.body:
## PARTITION BY and ORDER BY inside the window

Yesterday's windows ran over the whole table. Real reports almost always want windows **per group**, running total *per region*, rank *within each category*. That is what `PARTITION BY` does: it restarts the window for each group, like a `GROUP BY` that does not collapse rows.

The full window definition has two parts:
- **`PARTITION BY`** = which group to restart the calculation for.
- **`ORDER BY`** = the order within each group (required for running totals, ranking, LAG/LEAD).

```
SELECT region, order_date, sales,
  SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY order_date) AS region_running_total
FROM orders;
```
Now each region has its own running total that resets at the region boundary, exactly what a "sales to date by region" report needs.

Ranking within a group, the classic "top N per category":
```
SELECT category, product, total_sales,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY total_sales DESC) AS rank_in_cat
FROM product_sales;
```
Filter `rank_in_cat <= 3` (in an outer query or CTE) and you have the top 3 products in every category, a report that is genuinely awkward without window functions.

**The distinction to lock in:** `PARTITION BY` controls *grouping* (where the window resets), `ORDER BY` controls *sequence* (the order the function walks rows). `GROUP BY` collapses; `PARTITION BY` keeps every row. Mixing these up is the most common window-function bug. Write a "running total per region" and a "rank within category" today.

items.title: Complex aggregations
items.body:
## Complex aggregations for reporting

Beyond windows, reporting SQL leans on a few aggregation patterns that turn raw rows into the shapes a dashboard wants.

**Conditional aggregation** (the SQL pivot, count/sum only rows meeting a condition, in one pass):
```
SELECT region,
  SUM(sales) AS total_sales,
  SUM(CASE WHEN profit < 0 THEN sales ELSE 0 END) AS unprofitable_sales,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE profit < 0) AS loss_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;
```
`CASE` inside `SUM` (or `FILTER` in Postgres) lets one query produce many conditional metrics side by side, the backbone of summary tables.

**Multi-level totals with `GROUPING SETS` / `ROLLUP`** (subtotals and grand totals in one query):
```
SELECT region, category, SUM(sales)
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, category);
```
`ROLLUP` adds per-region subtotals and a grand total row, the kind of hierarchical summary managers expect.

**CTEs to stay readable.** Build reports in named steps with `WITH`:
```
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS mth, SUM(sales) AS sales
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT mth, sales,
  AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY mth ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS rolling_3m
FROM monthly;
```
This computes monthly sales, then a 3-month rolling average on top, the SQL twin of last week's DAX rolling measure. CTEs (`WITH`) are how analysts keep multi-step reporting queries legible instead of nesting subqueries into soup. Build a regional summary with conditional aggregation and a CTE today.

items.title: Query optimisation
items.body:
## Query optimisation (enough to not be dangerous)

A report query that takes 40 seconds makes a dashboard people abandon. You do not need to be a DBA, but a BI analyst should know enough to write queries that do not crawl, and to read why one does.

The handful of things that matter most:
- **Select only what you need.** `SELECT *` drags every column over the wire; name the columns you actually use.
- **Filter early and on indexed columns.** A `WHERE order_date >= '2018-01-01'` that uses an index on `order_date` reads a slice; without an index it scans the whole table. Date and key columns are the usual indexes.
- **Aggregate before you join when you can.** Joining two huge tables then aggregating is slower than aggregating each side down first (often via CTEs) then joining the small results.
- **Understand `EXPLAIN`.** Prefix a query with `EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) and the database shows its plan. The words to fear are "Seq Scan" on a big table where you expected an index. You do not need to read every line, just spot "is it scanning the whole table when it should not?".

The mental model: databases are fast when they can read a small, indexed slice and do little work; slow when forced to scan and sort everything. Most slow report queries are "no useful filter" or "filtering on an unindexed column". Run `EXPLAIN` on one of your window queries today and find the most expensive step, that habit alone puts you ahead of most self-taught analysts.

items.title: Views, materialised views, and stored procedures for BI
items.body:
## Views, materialised views, and stored procedures for BI

Once your reporting queries work, you do not want to paste them everywhere. SQL gives you ways to save and reuse logic, the analyst's equivalent of building a reusable measure.

- **View:** a saved query that behaves like a table. `CREATE VIEW monthly_sales AS SELECT ...`. Every time you query the view, the underlying SQL runs fresh, so it is always current, but it costs the full query each time. Use views to give Power BI / Looker a clean, business-friendly table (`monthly_sales`, `region_summary`) instead of raw tables, so the model layer stays simple and everyone uses the same definition of "sales".
- **Materialised view:** a view whose results are **stored** and refreshed on a schedule. `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ...`. Fast to read (it is precomputed), but can be stale until refreshed. Use it for expensive aggregations that do not need to be second-fresh, a nightly-refreshed summary that a dashboard reads instantly. (This is the SQL-side mirror of Power BI's scheduled refresh.)
- **Stored procedure:** saved, parameterised SQL logic you can call, `CALL refresh_reporting()`. In BI, stored procs often run the ETL/refresh steps that populate reporting tables.

The reporting pattern this enables: raw tables -> views/materialised views that define clean business metrics -> the BI tool reads those, not the raw mess. That separation (a "reporting layer" or "semantic layer" in SQL) is exactly what tools like dbt formalise (you will meet dbt in W8). Create a `region_summary` view over your `orders` table today and query it, that is the reusable, single-source-of-truth habit that scales BI past one analyst's head.

## Ship it

Package the week's SQL into a portfolio artefact: a `.sql` file of reporting queries that a hiring manager can read and immediately see you know analytics SQL.

Assemble a `superstore_reporting.sql` containing your best, commented queries from the week:
- a running total and a `LAG` period-over-period query,

- a CTE-based monthly rolling average,

Comment each query with one line on the business question it answers. Commit it to a repo (or your `superstore-bi` repo as a `/sql` folder) with a short README explaining the dataset and what each query demonstrates.

```
git add sql/superstore_reporting.sql && git commit -m "BI: SQL reporting - window functions, aggregations, reusable views"

```

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: WHERE and HAVING both filter rows, but they act at different moments in the query, and that timing is the whole point. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, it decides which raw rows even enter the calculation. HAVING filters after a GROUP BY has aggregated the rows, it decides which groups survive based on their aggregated values. So you cannot use WHERE to say 'only regions whose total sales exceed 100,000', because that total does not exist until after grouping, that is a HAVING job; but you can use WHERE to say 'only orders from 2024' before grouping. A query using both reads: WHERE filters the year, GROUP BY rolls up by region, HAVING keeps only the big-selling regions. Write me that query, and explain why moving the HAVING condition into WHERE would be a syntax or logic error.

weeks.title: Data Modelling and Warehouse Concepts
weeks.context:
Data warehousing is the backend of BI. When a company scales beyond Excel and Power BI files, they build a data warehouse, a centralised repository of integrated, historical data designed for analysis rather than transactions.

The key concepts: OLTP vs OLAP (transactional databases optimised for writes vs analytical databases optimised for reads), dimensional modelling (star and snowflake schemas), slowly changing dimensions (how to handle data that changes over time, like a customer's address), and fact table granularity (what exactly one row represents).

Modern data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks) have largely replaced traditional on-premise warehouses. They are columnar, massively parallel, and can query petabytes in seconds. Understanding how they differ from row-based databases explains why your SQL performance patterns are different.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: OLTP and OLAP are two database worlds optimised for opposite jobs, and confusing them is why some reports crawl. OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) powers the live application, many tiny, fast reads and writes, like 'insert this order' or 'update this customer', and is structured (highly normalised) to make those single-row operations safe and quick. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) powers analytics, a few enormous queries that scan and aggregate millions of rows, like 'total sales by region by month for three years', and is structured (star schemas, columnar storage) to make those sweeping aggregations fast. A query like that three-year roll-up flies on OLAP but crawls on OLTP, because OLTP was never built to scan everything. Give me one specific query that is fast on OLAP and slow on OLTP, and explain what about each design causes the difference.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Mean and median both try to capture 'the typical value', but they react very differently to extremes, and knowing which to trust is what separates an analyst from a calculator. The mean adds everything up and divides by the count, so every value pulls on it, including one giant outlier. The median is the middle value when you line the data up in order, so it ignores how extreme the extremes are. Picture salaries on a team where everyone earns around 50k except a founder on 5 million: the mean salary looks like several hundred thousand (a number nobody actually earns), while the median stays near 50k, the honest 'typical' figure. For skewed business data like income, deal size, or page-load times, the median usually tells the truer story. Give me a real business metric where reporting the mean would actively mislead a manager, and explain what the median reveals instead.

weeks.title: A/B Testing and Hypothesis Testing
weeks.context:
A/B testing is how data-driven companies make product decisions. Instead of debating which version of a feature is better, you run both versions simultaneously, collect data, and let statistics decide. A BI analyst's job in an A/B test: design the experiment correctly, analyse the results without bias, and communicate findings clearly.

The most common A/B testing mistakes are not statistical, they are design mistakes: running the test too short, stopping when you first see significance, testing too many variants simultaneously, and not defining the primary metric before the test starts. These mistakes produce false positives that lead companies to ship worse products.

This week you learn the statistics of A/B testing (two-sample tests, power analysis, sample size calculation) and how to run and analyse experiments using Python. You also learn the business side: how to communicate results to stakeholders who don't understand p-values.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Type I and Type II errors are the two ways a hypothesis test can fool you, and naming them is less useful than feeling their cost. A Type I error (false positive) is concluding there is an effect when there is not, in an A/B test, declaring the new button a winner and shipping it, when really it does nothing. A Type II error (false negative) is missing a real effect, killing a genuinely better variant because the test did not reach significance. Which hurts more depends entirely on the cost of the action: if shipping the change is cheap and reversible, a Type I error is survivable; if shipping it means a costly engineering commitment or a risk to revenue, a false positive is the expensive one. The skill is reasoning about consequences, not just probabilities. For a checkout-flow A/B test, tell me which error you would fear more and why.

weeks.title: KPIs, Metrics Design, and Data Storytelling
weeks.context:
A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a metric that measures progress toward a specific business objective. Most companies have too many KPIs, and most of them are vanity metrics, numbers that look good but don't tell you whether the business is healthy or how to improve it.

Good metrics have three properties: they are actionable (someone can change their behaviour based on them), they are comparable (you can tell if this week's number is good or bad by comparing to something), and they are understandable (the person being measured understands how the number is calculated).

Data storytelling is the practice of presenting data in a narrative that leads to a decision. The best BI analysts don't just produce charts, they answer "so what?" and "now what?". This week you learn both: how to design metrics that matter, and how to present them in a way that drives action.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Metric, KPI, and North Star metric are three nested levels of importance, and using the words loosely makes a strategy conversation mushy. A metric is any number you can measure, page views, signups, email opens; there are thousands. A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is the small subset of metrics you have decided actually indicate success against a goal, the ones you put on the dashboard and hold people to. A North Star metric is the single number that best captures the core value your product delivers and that the whole company rallies behind, for a SaaS company, perhaps 'weekly active teams' or 'monthly recurring revenue'. The hierarchy is: many metrics, few KPIs, one North Star. Give me an example of each for a SaaS business, and explain why elevating the wrong metric to North Star could steer the whole company astray.

weeks.title: Python for BI Analysts
weeks.context:
Python is not a replacement for Power BI, it is what you use when Power BI is not enough. Complex data transformations, custom visualisations, machine learning features, and automation are all significantly easier in Python than in any BI tool.

For a BI analyst, the Python toolkit is: pandas for data manipulation, matplotlib/seaborn/plotly for visualisation, and Jupyter notebooks for exploratory analysis and shareable reports. You are not writing production software, you are writing data analysis scripts that can be reviewed, rerun, and modified.

This week you learn the pandas operations that show up constantly in BI work: groupby, merge, pivot_table, apply, and time series resampling. These are the Python equivalents of SQL GROUP BY, JOIN, PIVOT, and window functions.
