items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: groupby().agg() and pivot_table() in pandas both summarise data, but they shape the output differently, and choosing the right one saves you a reshaping headache. groupby().agg() collapses rows into groups and returns a long, tidy result, one row per group, columns for your aggregations, which is ideal when you are feeding the result into more code or a chart. pivot_table() reshapes into a spreadsheet-style grid, spreading one variable across the columns, closer to what you would build in Excel, ideal for a human-readable cross-tab (sales by region down the side, by year across the top). pivot_table also handles aggregation and missing combinations gracefully. So: groupby for tidy, code-friendly summaries; pivot_table for grid-shaped, presentation-friendly cross-tabs. Give me one analysis where pivot_table is clearly the better choice and one where groupby().agg() is, and explain the difference in the shape you get back.

weeks.title: Cloud BI: Google Looker Studio and BigQuery
weeks.context:
Cloud BI tools, Google Looker Studio, AWS QuickSight, Tableau Cloud, have a different architecture from desktop tools like Power BI Desktop. Data lives in a cloud warehouse (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake), queries run in the cloud, and reports are web-based and collaborative. There is no .pbix file to email, the report is a URL.

BigQuery is Google's managed data warehouse and one of the best places to learn cloud BI because it has a free tier with 1TB of query processing per month. Looker Studio (formerly Google Data Studio) connects to BigQuery natively and is free. Together they give you a production-grade cloud BI stack at zero cost.

The key difference from desktop BI: in cloud BI, your data stays in the warehouse and you query it live (DirectQuery equivalent). This means SQL skills matter more, every visualisation is a SQL query under the hood.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS**, use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery**, use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Cloud warehouse**, use **DuckDB** or local **Postgres**: identical SQL, zero cost.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Looker Studio and Looker share a name and a parent (Google) but are very different products, and knowing why both exist tells you when to reach for each. Looker Studio (the old Data Studio) is the free, self-serve dashboarding tool, you connect a source, drag charts onto a canvas, share a link; great for fast reports and small teams. Looker (the enterprise platform Google acquired) is a heavyweight modelling layer built on LookML, where data teams define metrics once, centrally and governed, so the whole organisation queries consistent, trusted definitions, it is about governance and a single source of truth at scale. Google kept both because they serve opposite ends: ad-hoc and free versus governed and enterprise. Tell me which one a five-person startup reaches for versus a thousand-person company that needs everyone to agree on what 'revenue' means, and why.

weeks.title: AI-Assisted BI Workflows
weeks.context:
AI tools are now embedded in every major BI platform. Power BI Copilot, Tableau Pulse, Google Looker AI, and standalone tools like Julius.ai and Hex can generate charts, write DAX, explain data, and answer natural-language questions about your data. Ignoring these tools costs you productivity.

The skill is not using AI to replace your analysis, it is using AI to accelerate the mechanical parts (writing DAX, writing SQL, formatting charts) so you can spend more time on the parts that require human judgment (interpreting results, designing experiments, communicating to stakeholders).

This week you build an AI-assisted workflow: using Claude or ChatGPT to generate and debug DAX and SQL, using Power BI Copilot (if you have Pro access) for natural language report generation, and understanding where AI analysis should be verified and where it can be trusted.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: The honest answer to 'what should AI do in BI' is: AI is excellent at the mechanical and the first-draft, and weak at judgment and context. Well-suited tasks: drafting a DAX or SQL query from a plain-English description (you still verify it), explaining an unfamiliar function or error, and generating boilerplate like documentation or repetitive transformations, work where the answer is checkable and the cost of a wrong draft is low. Tasks that need human judgment: deciding which metric actually matters to the business, interpreting whether a result is meaningful or an artifact of bad data, and any call where being confidently wrong has real consequences. The pattern: AI accelerates the typing; you own the thinking. Give me three BI tasks you would happily delegate to AI and three you would never, and explain the line that separates them.

weeks.title: BI Portfolio and Interview Preparation
weeks.context:
A BI portfolio is your proof of work. Anyone can list Power BI and SQL on a CV, very few people can show a dashboard, explain the design decisions, and walk through the DAX or SQL behind it. Those people get the interviews.

Your BI portfolio should demonstrate three things: technical skills (can you build a complete, well-structured Power BI report or SQL pipeline?), analytical thinking (can you find interesting insights and explain why they matter?), and communication (can you present data in a way that drives decisions?).

This week you package everything you have built into a portfolio, prepare for common interview question types (technical SQL/DAX questions, case study analysis, stakeholder communication scenarios), and practise until the answers are fluent.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Walking an interviewer through your most complex DAX measure is really a test of whether you understand your own work or just got it to run. Pick a genuinely non-trivial measure, say a year-over-year growth percentage, or a rank-within-category, or a dynamic measure switched by a slicer, and structure your answer in three beats. First, what it calculates in business terms ('this shows each product's sales growth versus the same month last year'). Second, why the key functions are there, why CALCULATE was needed to override or set the filter context, why you used a VAR to capture a value before the context shifted. Third, how you tested it, the known month you hand-checked, the edge case (first year, blank periods) you confirmed. The interviewer is listening for whether you can explain the filter-context reasoning, not recite syntax. Pick a real measure and give me that three-part walkthrough now.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: The most important insight from your capstone is the one sentence a stakeholder would remember a week later, and being able to state it, with honest confidence, is the whole point of the project. So give it to me sharply: not 'sales vary by region' but 'the West region's margin is being silently eroded by discounting, and it is the single biggest drag on company profit'. Then do the thing that separates an analyst from a chart-maker: tell me how confident you are and why. What is the strength of the evidence, and just as importantly, what would invalidate it, a data-quality issue, a confounding variable, too small a sample, a correlation you have not proven causal? State your single most important insight, your confidence level, and the specific finding or error that would overturn it.
